gi10_authentic.topic: Authentic but narrow items: Genesis 15:18, Herzl's 1898 diary note, the 1919 ZO boundary statement, Rabbi Fishman's 1947 UNSCOP answer

claims.text: Pipes (MEQ 1994), the writer most cited as debunking the Herzl item, himself reports that in 1898 Herzl 'planned to ask the Ottoman sultan for a territory stretching from the Egyptian frontier to the Euphrates' (Zionistische Tagebuecher vol. 2 p. 650) and that Herzl 'did not in fact request' it from anyone; the note is authentic, the request and programme are not.
Genesis 15:18 (KJV): 'Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates'; NIV renders 'from the Wadi of Egypt'.
Encyclopedia of The Bible reads 'river of Egypt' (nahar) as the Nile, while nahal Mitzrayim, the 'brook of Egypt' of the boundary texts, is 'highly probably' Wadi el-Arish.

ZO Statement to the Paris Peace Conference, 3 Feb 1919: north boundary from 'a point on the Mediterranean Sea in the vicinity south of Sidon', Hermon slopes; east 'a line close to and west of the Hedjaz Railway terminating in the Gulf of Akaba'; south 'a frontier to be agreed upon with the Egyptian Government'; no Sinai, no Euphrates, no Damascus.

JTA dispatch (Detroit Jewish News, 18 July 1947): before UNSCOP, Indian delegate Sir Abdur Rahman asked Mizrachi leader Rabbi Judah L. Fishman, 'What were the boundaries of the land promised by God to the Jews?'; Fishman answered 'From Egypt to the Euphrates', said 'God promised it to Abraham 4,000 years ago', and that the promise was to Isaac's descendants: 'He gave Ishmael another land.' The Nile is not mentioned.
Pipes argues the Genesis covenant includes Ishmael's descendants and that the specific boundary passages (Numbers 34, Ezekiel 47) govern the general promise.

gi10_misread.topic: Misread documents: the Yinon essay (1982), A Clean Break (1996), the 10-agora coin

claims.text: Yinon's essay appeared in Kivunim no. 14 (Feb 1982), pp. 49-59, a quarterly published 1978-87 by the WZO Department of Information; Yinon reputedly a former adviser to Ariel Sharon, former senior Foreign Ministry official and Jerusalem Post journalist; Shahak's translation appeared in the Journal of Palestine Studies (1982) as 'Making the Arab World Collapse'.

In the Shahak translation Yinon writes that '(Regaining) the Sinai peninsula with its present and potential resources is therefore a political priority', obstructed by Camp David, but that 'Israel will not unilaterally break the treaty'; 'Syria will fall apart, in accordance with its ethnic and religious structure'; 'Lebanon's total dissolution into five provinces serves as a precendent'. The translator's note says it was disseminated on 13 June 1982. The online copy is partial.

Per Wikipedia, the only explicit territorial aim for Israel itself in the essay is restoring control of Sinai; it called for the 'liquidation' of Jordan as a Hashemite state with West Bank Palestinians moved east; Israel did not re-enter Sinai.

Reception: Nisan - Yinon's views alone, not policy; Harkabi - why interfere if fragmentation inevitable; Peleg - 'an authentic mirror of the thinking mode of the Israeli Right'; Chomsky linked it to Tehiya; Becker and Polkinghorn (2017) argue it was refined in A Clean Break. Later conspiracy uses tie it to the 2003 Iraq war, the Syrian civil war and ISIS (TheMarker, 8 Feb 2016); Arab News (Heard, 29 Nov 2005) said the plan was 'in large part taking shape'; Garaudy used it in 1983; Yinon replied in 1983 he was not a supporter of Sharon or Begin.

A Clean Break's territorial content: proposed speech text 'Our claim to the land - to which we have clung for hope for 2000 years - is legitimate and noble'; 'Only the unconditional acceptance by Arabs of our rights, especially in their territorial dimension, "peace for peace,"' is a solid basis; recommends 'rejecting "land for peace" deals on the Golan Heights'; 'redrawing of the map of the Middle East' appears as Syria's fear ('could be the prelude to'); the text does not mention the West Bank, Judea and Samaria or settlements.

Arafat at a specially convened UN Security Council session in Geneva, 25 May 1990, said the 10-agora coin showed a 'map of Greater Israel'; he drew on Gwyn Rowley's 1989 GeoJournal paper, which said the coin's shape 'seemingly' resembled an area reaching Amman, Beirut, Baghdad and Damascus; S.M. Berkowicz (GeoJournal 1991) called the claim undocumented with 'no foundation'.

Bank of Israel: the 10 agorot obverse is a 'Replica of a coin issued by Mattathias Antigonus (37 - 40 B.C.E.) with the seven-branched candelabrum'; issued 4 Sept 1985; obverse designer Nathan Karp. The design first appeared on the 100-sheqel coin of 2 May 1984.

Pipes: Arafat to the Arab League Jerusalem Committee, 9 Apr 1990, said the map was 'directly under' the menorah; Israel Museum's Ya'akov Meshorer said 'Karp was astounded ... that anyone could see the coast of the Land of Israel there' (Jerusalem Post, 9 June 1990).

CRS (5 Nov 1998): 'Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian Authority Chairman Yasir Arafat signed the Wye River Memorandum'; 'Wye requires Israel to transfer 13% of Area (C) to the Palestinians' (1% to Area A, 12% to Area B) and 14.2% from Area B to Area A; Israel redeployed from Hebron after the Protocol of 17 January 1997.

gi10_myths.topic: Myths: the Knesset 'Nile to Euphrates' inscription and the flag's stripes as rivers; how the claims circulated

claims.text: Christian Science Monitor correction, 28 Jan 1980: its 21 Jan story 'Egyptians dispute Sadat bid to give Nile water to Israel' attributed the slogan 'From the Nile to the Euphrates' to the Israeli parliament building; 'No such inscription is on the building.'

Pipes: Syria's Hafiz al-Asad and defence minister Mustafa Tlas and Iran's president said 'The Land of Israel from the Euphrates to the Nile' is chiselled over the Knesset entrance (Al-Jazira, 17 Jan 1982); a visitor who sees no such map is told 'it was removed in anticipation of his visit'; Arafat (Arab League Jerusalem Committee, 9 Apr 1990) said a sign 'remained for ten years' and had been put back.

The Knesset's own description of its Chagall State Hall lists three Gobelin tapestries, 12 floor mosaics and one wall mosaic with biblical and ingathering themes; it records no map or border inscription.

Israel MFA: 'The blue stripes on the Zionist flag were inspired by the stripes on the tallit (prayer shawl)'; Zionist tradition credits the design to David Wolffsohn; the flag was adopted by the Zionist movement in Basel (MFA: First Congress, 1897); the Provisional Council of State 'voted unanimously on October 28, 1948' to adopt it as the state flag.

Wolffsohn wrote: 'The talith (prayer shawl) with which we wrap ourselves when we pray: that is our symbol'; Rishon LeZion used a blue-and-white Star of David flag in 1885; Frankl's poem 'Juda's Farben' (1864) proposed blue and white as Jewish colours.
Arafat told Playboy (Sept 1988) the two blue lines represent the Nile and Euphrates 'and in between is Israel'; Pipes: the lines derive from the prayer shawl design.
Hamas Covenant, Article 32 (18 Aug 1988): 'After Palestine, the Zionists aspire to expand from the Nile to the Euphrates.'
Saqr Abu Fakhr (Al-Hayat, Nov 1997) called the Nile-to-Euphrates belief an unfounded popular misconception about Jews.

claims.text: JTA (DJN 18 July 1947): after Fishman answered 'From Egypt to the Euphrates', Sir Abdur Rahman asked whether that included Egypt, Syria and Lebanon, Iraq, India, Transjordan; Fishman answered 'No' to each.
Rowley replied to Berkowicz that the coin may have been chosen because of its map-like shape; the Bank of Israel says the design was chosen for its historical value.

Pipes: at the Arab League committee on 9 April 1990 Arafat said the Knesset sign 'remained for ten years' and had been restored; days later he changed his account, saying the plaque had been removed and the map engraved on the coin instead.
